notes.meaning: A synagogue leader named Jairus begs Jesus with deep love and concern for his dying daughter. He asks Jesus to come and place His hands on her so that she might recover and live. Jairus truly believes Jesus has the power to heal her, even though he thinks Jesus must be physically present to do it.
Jesus immediately goes with Jairus toward his home. A massive crowd follows along, crowding and bumping into Him so tightly that He can hardly move.

In the crowd is a woman who has suffered from continuous bleeding for twelve years. According to Jewish law, this sickness made her unclean, which meant she was cut off from normal worship and community life. Her long suffering began around the same time Jairus's daughter was born.

The woman had tried many doctors and endured many painful treatments over the years. She spent all her money trying to get well, but nothing helped at all. Instead of improving, her illness only grew worse, leaving her completely helpless.

Having heard reports about Jesus and His miracles, she comes up behind Him in the pressing crowd. She reaches out and touches the edge of His outer robe. She comes quietly from behind because she is ashamed of her illness and afraid of being noticed.

She kept telling herself that she did not even need to speak to Jesus or have Him touch her. She believed that touching just His clothes would be enough to make her well. Even though her understanding was simple and a bit timid, she trusted fully in the power of Jesus.

The moment she touches His robe, her bleeding stops completely. She can feel in her own body right away that the painful sickness is entirely gone. Jesus instantly cures what twelve years of human medicine could not fix.

Jesus realizes at once within Himself that healing power has gone out from Him. He turns around in the middle of the crowd and asks who touched His clothes. He asks not because He is ignorant, but because He wants to bring her faith into the open.

The disciples are surprised by the question, seeing how many people are shoving against Him. They point out that in such a tight pack, people are bumping into Him from every side. But they do not yet realize the difference between people casually jostling Him and someone reaching out in true faith.

Jesus pays no attention to their objection and keeps looking around the crowd to see who touched Him. He searches for the person whose faith had drawn on His power. He wants to meet her face-to-face and encourage her openly.

The woman realizes she cannot stay hidden and comes forward trembling with fear. She falls on her knees before Jesus and openly confesses the whole story of her illness and cure. Jesus receives her kindly, proving that those who come to Him need never be afraid.

Jesus tenderly calls her "Daughter" and tells her that her trust in Him has made her well. He confirms that her cure is real and permanent, telling her to go in peace and be free from her sickness. His warm words assure her that she is fully accepted and forgiven.

While Jesus is still speaking with the woman, people arrive from Jairus's house with bad news. They tell the father that his little girl has died, so there is no point in troubling the Teacher any longer. They assume death has ended all hope, since they view Jesus only as a healer for the living.

Jesus overhears what the messengers say and immediately speaks words of comfort to Jairus. He tells the grieving father not to give way to fear, but simply to keep trusting Him. Jesus shows that human despair is never the end of what God can do.

Jesus stops the crowd and allows only Peter, James, and John to go with Him to the house. He keeps the group small so there will be reliable witnesses without creating a wild public scene. These three close followers are chosen to see His greatest acts of power.

When they reach the house, Jesus sees loud confusion and mourners weeping and wailing noisily. It was customary at that time to hire mourners and musicians to make loud, public displays of grief when someone died. The house is filled with uproar rather than quiet sorrow.

Jesus enters and asks why they are making such noisy grief. He tells them the little girl is not dead, but asleep. To Jesus, her death is only temporary, no harder for Him to wake her from than an ordinary nap.

The mourners laugh at Jesus in scorn because they are certain the girl is truly dead. Jesus makes all of them leave the house, refusing to let mockers witness His holy work. He then takes only the girl's parents and His three disciples into the room where she lies.

Jesus gently takes the dead child by the hand and speaks to her in Aramaic, the common everyday language of the land. He says, "Talitha koum," which means, "Little girl, I say to you, get up!" His voice carries divine authority that even death must obey.

Immediately the twelve-year-old girl gets out of bed and begins walking around the room. Her return to life is sudden, complete, and fully visible to everyone present. Her parents and the disciples are completely stunned with wonder at what Jesus has done.

Jesus strictly warns the parents not to spread the news everywhere, and He tells them to give the girl food. He wants to avoid wild crowds and premature hostility before His appointed time has come. Giving her food shows she is genuinely alive and healthy, while reminding us that God cares for our everyday physical needs.
